title: The brothers bow (Genesis 42)
hookLine: his brothers come for grain and don't recognize him; he turns away and weeps

cards: The good years come, and Joseph fills the storehouses. Then the famine arrives, as the dreams said, all the way to Canaan, where old Jacob watches his family go hungry.
He hears there's grain in Egypt: why do you just sit looking at one another? Go down and buy some. Ten brothers go.

Benjamin, Rachel's other son, stays home. Jacob has already lost one of Rachel's boys; he won't risk the second. So ten men walk into Egypt to stand in line for bread, before the governor of the land.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Joseph's brethren came, and bowed down themselves before him with their faces to the earth." The sheaves are bowing, and Joseph remembered the dreams, the text says.

teach.h: HE KNEW THEM; THEY KNEW NOT HIM.
teach.b: "Joseph knew his brethren, but they knew not him." Of course not. He was a teenager in a coat; now he's a grown Egyptian official, shaved, speaking through an interpreter.
He speaks roughly, accuses them of being spies, and holds them three days. Then he lets them go, but keeps one brother, Simeon, bound, until they come back with the youngest.

And the brothers, not knowing he understands every word, talk among themselves in their own language: "We are verily guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the anguish of his soul, when he besought us, and we would not hear."
All these years later, the pit is still in the room. Then: "And he turned himself about from them, and wept."

teach.h: THE GOVERNOR TURNS AWAY AND WEEPS.
teach.b: The governor steps away so no one sees his face, cries, and comes back to keep testing them.

teach.h: AND HE TURNED HIMSELF ABOUT FROM THEM, AND WEPT.
teach.b: Why test them? Genesis doesn't say. Readers wonder whether he wants to know if they've changed, or is simply hurt and doesn't know what to do yet.

Genesis leaves both open. Look at the week behind us: Esau running to his brother, the coat, the pit, Potiphar's house, the forgotten prisoner, the dreams by the Nile. Under all of it sits a family that broke.
And now the brothers say out loud what they did.

how: Some Christians read Genesis 42 as a story about guilt surfacing years later, and preachers use the brothers' confession to talk about honesty and repentance within families.

games.q: you're Joseph. the brothers who sold you are bowing at your feet, and they don't know you. you understand every word they say to each other. what do you do?
o: tell them who you are at once.
speak roughly, test them, and turn away to weep.
have them all thrown in prison for good.
games.why: he accuses them of spying, keeps Simeon, and sends them for Benjamin. and when he hears them admit their guilt, he turns away and weeps.

practice: Maybe there was a time you turned away so no one would see you cry: at work, at a funeral, in the car before walking into the house.
You don't have to cry now; just notice what was being carried then, and how long it was carried alone, and let your shoulders drop.
If you pray, you can bring that moment to God; if you don't, be gentle with the person you were then.

wordCard.voice: Simeon. The brother Joseph holds back in Egypt, kept bound until the others return with their youngest brother.

orig.note: Hebrew: to weep. Joseph weeps again and again in the chapters that follow.
